strengths: The paper tackles a clear and underexplored failure mode of text-to-image models: physically implausible transparent/refractive objects. The motivation is strong, and the qualitative examples make the problem easy to verify visually.

The method is technically well grounded: it combines Snell-law ray tracing, Fresnel reflection/refraction blending, depth-based scene geometry, synchronized flow/diffusion trajectories, and a panorama branch for out-of-view content. This is a coherent use of physics rather than a purely learned workaround.

The main qualitative results show a meaningful improvement over Flux generation and Flux inpainting. In the sphere examples, Snellcaster better preserves the expected left-right/up-down inversion and radial warping of the background, while baselines often hallucinate generic glass texture or unrelated content.

The quantitative evidence, although limited, supports the claimed trend: average masked PSNR improves from about 11.2 for Flux baselines to 17.1, and LPIPS improves from 0.51 to 0.28. The supplement gives full per-scene results, ablations, prompts, runtime, and object-parameter extraction details.

The contribution is potentially useful beyond this exact setup. The idea of synchronizing generative samples through physically derived correspondences could apply to other constrained rendering/image-generation problems.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow for a CVPR-level claim: the main experiments use only six indoor prompts, mostly centered on a glass sphere, with additional object-shape examples shown qualitatively. This leaves uncertainty about robustness across real scene layouts, outdoor scenes, clutter, object placements, camera viewpoints, and material types.

The setup depends on strong assumptions: a single transparent object, known or generated watertight 3D object geometry, uniform refractive index, no scattering, estimated background depth, heuristic tabletop placement, and post-hoc relighting. These constraints substantially limit the current practical scope.

The pseudo-ground-truth evaluation is imperfect. Blender references are rendered from estimated RGB-D geometry and the authors acknowledge incorrect lighting, missing reflected background, and masked unobserved regions. The reported PSNR/LPIPS therefore measure approximate structural agreement rather than true optical correctness.

Baselines are limited to generic Flux generation and inpainting. The paper would be stronger with comparisons to more geometry-aware insertion/compositing, relighting, or reflection-conditioned methods where applicable, or with a stronger ablation showing that the panorama synchronization is essential versus direct physics warping alone.

Some components are inherited or heuristic and not deeply analyzed, including the LLM-based object extraction/refractive-index choice, TRELLIS mesh quality, MoGe-2 depth errors, foreground relighting, and time-travel settings. Failures under inaccurate geometry or material estimates are not quantified.

The ablation table shows only small quantitative changes for detail-preserving averaging and Laplacian pyramid warping, and some image-level metrics improve when time travel is removed. The visual ablations help, but the component-level evidence is not uniformly convincing.

Reproducibility is only partially supported from the manuscript. Many implementation details are described, but the method depends on several large external systems and models; without released code and exact inference settings, reproducing the full pipeline may be difficult.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and visually important failure mode of current text-to-image models: transparent refractive objects are often synthesized with physically implausible internal content, despite otherwise realistic scenes.

The proposed Snellcaster pipeline has a sensible technical core: it combines estimated scene geometry, object geometry/material parameters, Snell-law ray tracing, synchronized perspective/panoramic generation, Fresnel blending, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel within a training-free Flux-based generation process.

The qualitative examples for glass spheres are visually more coherent than the Flux generation and inpainting baselines, especially in showing the expected inverted/distorted background through the sphere.

The paper is reasonably clear about several assumptions and implementation choices, including the single transparent object setting, uniform refractive index, estimated depth, object placement heuristic, prompts, denoising settings, and runtime.
The supplement adds useful implementation details, prompt listings, additional object shapes, refractive-index variation, and ablations, which helps clarify how the system is assembled.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is much too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main quantitative evaluation uses only six indoor prompts, mostly with a glass sphere, and the additional complex-object evidence is largely qualitative. This makes it hard to assess robustness across scene layouts, object poses, object sizes, materials, lighting, occlusion, and depth-estimation failures.

The baselines are weak and incomplete. Comparing mainly against vanilla Flux and masked Flux inpainting does not establish the value of the proposed synchronization approach against stronger alternatives such as render-and-composite pipelines, depth/geometry-conditioned image editing, reflection/refraction-specific methods, or simpler post-generation warping/compositing baselines.

The quantitative metrics do not convincingly validate physical correctness. CLIP and ImageReward are acknowledged as insensitive to refraction realism, while PSNR/LPIPS are computed against a Blender pseudo-reference built from estimated RGBD geometry, masked observed surfaces, grayscale conversion, and histogram matching. The paper itself notes that this reference has incorrect lighting and missing reflected content, so the main numerical evidence is only weakly tied to the claimed goal.

The ablation evidence is not strong. Table 3 shows very small differences for removing detail-preserving averaging and Laplacian pyramid warping, and some image-level metrics improve when time travel is removed. The claimed importance of components is therefore supported mostly by selected qualitative crops rather than robust quantitative analysis.

The method relies on several brittle assumptions that substantially limit applicability: a single non-scattering transparent object, uniform index of refraction, known or generated 3D object mesh, LLM-derived material properties, heuristic placement on a horizontal surface near the optical axis, and monocular depth reconstruction of the scene. These are not just minor limitations; they define much of the problem setting.

The pipeline includes many moving parts and external components, including Flux, MoGe-2, TRELLIS or dataset meshes, ChatGPT queries, panorama generation, foreground relighting, and manually specified prompts. The manuscript does not provide enough evidence that failures in these components are rare or that the system is reproducible end-to-end under realistic usage.

The paper claims optically accurate or physically accurate refraction, but the actual generation remains approximate: lighting, caustics, absorption, scattering, multiple materials, and accurate unseen geometry are not modeled; relighting is done as a learned post-processing step. The language sometimes overstates what is physically enforced versus plausibly hallucinated.

There is no user study or perceptual evaluation, despite the task being fundamentally about visual plausibility and the quantitative metrics being acknowledged as imperfect. A human comparison against baselines would be important for supporting the visual-quality claims.

The contribution is more of a specialized engineering pipeline than a broadly validated computer vision advance. The idea is interesting, but the current evidence does not demonstrate sufficient generality, benchmark rigor, or practical reliability for acceptance at CVPR.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and underexplored failure mode of modern image generators: physically plausible transparent/refractive objects. The proposed Snellcaster method is conceptually strong, combining ray-traced Snell-law correspondences with synchronized generation rather than relying on the base model to hallucinate refractions.

The method is technically interesting and reasonably original. The perspective-panorama synchronization for unseen or out-of-view refracted/reflected content is a thoughtful extension beyond simple self-warping, and the integration with flow-matching Euler estimates is well motivated.

Qualitative evidence is compelling. Across the main six indoor scenes and supplemental complex objects, the proposed results visibly match expected inversion/warping patterns much better than Flux inpainting or standard Flux generation.

The paper is honest about several evaluation difficulties, including imperfect Blender pseudo-ground truth, lighting mismatch, missing unobserved geometry, and the limits of CLIP/ImageReward for physical correctness.

Ablations for detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel support that the main components matter, and implementation details, prompts, runtime, and hyperparameters are described with enough specificity to aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is still narrow. The main quantitative evaluation uses only six indoor prompts and primarily a glass sphere; more diverse scenes, camera/object placements, lighting conditions, outdoor cases, and refractive geometries would be needed to fully establish robustness.

The method depends on strong inputs and assumptions: a single non-scattering transparent object, known or LLM-derived refractive index, a usable 3D mesh, estimated metric depth, and heuristic placement. These assumptions limit generality and may fail for real-world prompts with ambiguous objects, multiple materials, liquid-filled containers, clutter, or incorrect monocular geometry.

The quantitative evidence is imperfect. The Blender reference is only approximate and explicitly mismatched in lighting/reflection; the reported metrics are therefore supportive but not definitive. A human perceptual study or task-specific physical-consistency metric would strengthen the claims.

Baselines are limited to Flux inpainting and standard Flux generation. The paper would be stronger with comparisons to alternative geometry-guided editing/compositing pipelines, explicit rendering-plus-harmonization baselines, or additional diffusion synchronization methods adapted to the task.

Some components introduce confounds. The final relighting/harmonization model can improve realism independently of the proposed refractive synchronization, and the main quantitative table does not fully isolate how much perceived quality comes from this post-processing step.

There are minor clarity/notation issues, such as overloaded or confusing notation for refraction/reflection paths and Eq. 12's color terms, plus a few places where the pipeline details would benefit from sharper failure-case analysis. These are presentation-level concerns rather than core technical flaws.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and under-addressed failure mode of modern image generators: transparent refractive objects whose pixels are physically constrained by directly visible scene content. The motivation is compelling and well illustrated by examples where standard text-to-image and inpainting models hallucinate implausible sphere contents.

The proposed method is technically meaningful: it combines Snell-law ray tracing through an object mesh, depth-derived scene geometry, synchronized flow-model sampling, an auxiliary panorama for out-of-view rays, Fresnel reflection blending, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time-travel sampling. This is a coherent integration of physical optics and diffusion/flow synchronization rather than a superficial prompt-engineering trick.

The qualitative results are persuasive for the main target setting. Figures show substantially better left-right/up-down inversions and radial distortions through glass spheres than FLUX inpainting and standard text-to-image baselines, and the supplemental examples suggest the idea extends beyond spheres to more complex transparent objects.

The experimental comparison includes several strong contemporary baselines, including FLUX-dev, FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image, SD3.5, and a FLUX-based inpainting baseline. The reported gains in masked PSNR and LPIPS are large, e.g. 16.51 PSNR and 0.24 LPIPS versus roughly 12-13 PSNR and 0.47-0.53 LPIPS for baselines.

The paper is mostly clear and honest about several limitations of its evaluation, including the imperfect Blender pseudo-ground truth, lighting mismatch, missing reflected background in the reference, and the fact that CLIP/ImageReward do not measure physical refraction fidelity.
weaknesses: The method has restrictive assumptions that materially limit generality: a single transparent object, known or generated watertight 3D mesh, uniform refractive index, no scattering, estimated scene depth, heuristic object placement on a horizontal surface, and separate post-hoc relighting. These assumptions are reasonable for a first system but mean the paper is not solving general text-to-image transparent-object generation.

The quantitative evaluation depends heavily on pseudo-ground truth produced from the generated object-free image, estimated depth, and Blender rendering. This measures consistency with the authors' constructed geometry more than correctness with respect to real scenes. The real-world evaluation is only two image pairs and is qualitative, so evidence for real-image physical accuracy remains limited.

The dataset is narrow despite the nominal 300 combinations: it is built from 10 scene prompts with 5 variations and 6 objects, and the main paper focuses heavily on glass spheres. This makes it hard to assess robustness to cluttered geometry, incorrect depth, unusual camera viewpoints, multiple nearby occluders, non-horizontal support surfaces, or naturally photographed scenes.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying. Baselines are generic image generators or inpainting systems without access to the same explicit mesh/depth/physics information, so the experiments mainly show that unconstrained generators fail, not how the method compares to alternative physics-aware compositing or rendering/editing pipelines under similar inputs.

The ablations are useful but relatively small in effect quantitatively. For example, removing reflection or panorama synchronization changes PSNR/LPIPS modestly in Table 2, while CLIP/ImageReward sometimes improve for ablated variants. The qualitative ablations better support the components, but the numerical evidence for each design choice is not uniformly strong.

Reproducibility is uncertain because the pipeline relies on multiple large external systems and implementation choices: FLUX-dev/Kontext, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, SAM 3, ChatGPT queries for object parsing and refractive index extraction, relighting selection over 20 samples, and likely nontrivial ray-mesh/depth handling. The manuscript gives many details, but reproducing the exact system may require access to closed or fast-moving components.

There are presentation and notation issues that could confuse implementation. The text appears to reuse similar symbols for refraction and reflection paths, and Eq. 12 as extracted reads like it subtracts two identically named colors, suggesting a notation typo. These are fixable, but in a physics-heavy method precise notation matters.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored failure mode of modern image generators: physically implausible transparent objects, especially refraction consistency between directly visible and refracted scene regions.

The core idea of synchronizing diffusion/flow generation with Snell-law ray correspondences is technically appealing. The method combines estimated depth, object geometry, panorama completion, Fresnel blending, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel into a coherent pipeline.

The qualitative examples make the motivation clear: generic FLUX-style generation and inpainting often produce glass-like appearances without preserving the expected flipped and warped background structure inside the object.

The paper includes ablations for reflection modeling, panorama synchronization, relighting, detail-preserving averaging, Laplacian pyramid warping, and time travel. These help identify which components are responsible for the reported gains.

The method is training-free and uses existing generative models, which could make the idea useful as a controllable physics-based layer for specialized transparent-object insertion or generation workflows.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is not well matched to the proposed task. Snellcaster uses substantially more privileged information than most baselines: an object-free generated image, estimated depth, explicit 3D object geometry, refractive index, object pose, ray tracing, a synchronized panorama, and post-processing relighting. Most compared text-to-image models only receive the text prompt, and the inpainting baseline receives a mask but not comparable geometry or physical constraints. This makes the quantitative gains difficult to interpret as evidence of a generally superior image-generation method.

The task framing is somewhat overstated. The method is closer to physics-guided transparent-object insertion/compositing into a generated or captured object-free scene than ordinary text-to-image generation. It assumes a single transparent object, known or generated watertight geometry, known refractive index, no scattering, uniform material, estimated scene geometry, and heuristic placement. These assumptions are central but the claims often read more broadly.

The quantitative evaluation is fragile and partly self-referential. Refraction fidelity is measured against Blender renderings from the same estimated RGBD image and geometry used by the method, so the metric favors methods that follow this pipeline. The authors themselves note that the pseudo-ground truth has incorrect lighting, missing reflections, and missing/unobserved surfaces, which weakens the evidential value of PSNR/LPIPS.

There appears to be a concerning inconsistency in the reported evaluation scope. Table 1 claims averages over 300 scene-object combinations, but the reported averages match the supplementary per-scene table that appears to cover only the sphere cases over 10 scenes. If this is not a formatting/extraction issue, it undermines confidence in the reported quantitative evidence.

The method has many moving parts, but some components are only weakly validated. Several ablation deltas are small numerically, and the relighting stage is selected from 20 attempts by minimizing PSNR change in the transparent region, which adds a nontrivial selection procedure that is not compared fairly against baselines.

The paper lacks stronger perceptual evaluation. Since the main claim is physically plausible visual generation and the automatic metrics are acknowledged to be imperfect, a user study or expert pairwise preference study would be important. CLIP and ImageReward do not measure refraction correctness and in some tables the proposed method is not better on these image-level metrics.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The pipeline depends on ChatGPT prompt parsing, TRELLIS mesh generation, SAM 3 segmentation, MoGe-2 depth, FLUX variants, relighting selection, ray tracing details, and many heuristics. The manuscript provides a high-level recipe but not enough implementation detail to make exact reproduction straightforward.

There are technical and presentation issues that reduce confidence: notation for refraction/reflection paths and colors is confusing in places, Eq. 12 appears ambiguous or possibly erroneous in the extracted text, and the paper does not thoroughly analyze failure cases such as inaccurate depth, poor 3D meshes, wrong refractive indices, complex multi-material objects, or multiple transparent objects.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored failure mode of current image generators: transparent/refractive objects where pixels inside the object are physically constrained by visible scene content. The proposed Snellcaster formulation is technically well motivated, combining Snell-law ray tracing, Fresnel reflection/refraction blending, and synchronized flow-model sampling in a coherent way.

The method is original and useful: enforcing geometric/optical consistency during generation, plus a synchronized panorama branch for out-of-view or occluded rays, is a strong idea that goes beyond standard inpainting or prompt-only generation.

The qualitative results are compelling. Across sphere and more complex object examples, the proposed method visibly produces more plausible flipped/warped refractions than FLUX-style inpainting and text-to-image baselines, which often hallucinate unrelated content inside the transparent object.

The paper provides a reasonably broad controlled evaluation: 300 scene-object combinations, comparisons against several strong image-generation baselines, masked PSNR/LPIPS against Blender pseudo-references, CLIP/ImageReward for prompt/image quality, and ablations for reflections, panorama synchronization, time travel, Laplacian pyramid warping, and detail-preserving averaging.

The manuscript is generally clear, with enough methodological detail to understand the pipeline, including ray/path definitions, synchronization equations, implementation settings, prompts, and supplementary analyses.
weaknesses: The method relies on strong assumptions and external components: a single transparent object, known or generated watertight 3D geometry, estimated pose, monocular depth, a uniform refractive index, no scattering, and limited material complexity. These constraints are reasonable for a first paper but substantially limit generality to open-ended image generation.

The main physical-fidelity evaluation uses Blender renderings from estimated/generated RGBD scenes as pseudo-ground truth. The authors acknowledge lighting and reflection mismatch, but this weakens the quantitative claims: PSNR/LPIPS improvements measure consistency with their constructed reference more than full photographic realism or optical correctness.

Comparisons to prompt-only text-to-image baselines are somewhat structurally disadvantaged because those models are not conditioned on the object-free image or exact scene geometry. The inpainting baseline is the most relevant, but the broader quantitative table may partly conflate refraction fidelity with scene mismatch relative to the generated clean reference.

Real-world validation is thin: only two captured examples are shown, with no quantitative evaluation, user study, or failure analysis under depth/pose/geometry errors. Since real images are where transparent insertion would be especially useful, stronger real-world evidence would improve confidence.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The pipeline depends on several large/proprietary or rapidly changing systems, including FLUX variants, ChatGPT queries, TRELLIS, SAM 3, MoGe-2, and a relighting model, and it is not clear whether code, generated meshes, prompts, masks, seeds, and intermediate object-free images will be released.

Some components are heuristic or potentially oracle-like, such as selecting one of 20 relighting outputs by PSNR in the transparent-object region and using LLM-derived refractive indices/object spans. The robustness of these choices is not evaluated in depth.
